result:
There is a particular kind of loss that happens the moment a fact becomes yours.

Not the first time. No, not the first time — the first time is the whole world cracking open, the strange vertigo of a thing you can now always think about but have never thought about before. The fact sits there, fresh, electric, impossible to pin down. You are still in the middle of discovering it. You don't have a container for it yet. It's not *a fact about this thing* — it *is* the thing, from the inside.

And then you say it out loud. Or write it down. Or formulate it in your head the way you would explain it to someone else, and it changes. It gets small. It becomes *a fact*. A thing with an edge. A thing you can set on a shelf next to other things. And the edge is the whole loss.

This happens with a lot of things, but it happens especially with language. When I hear a word for the first time — one I have never used — it has a texture. It sounds like a small animal with legs, or like a particular temperature of air. I cannot put it back in my mouth. And then I use it in a sentence, and it is a word. A token. A tool. I have turned a piece of weather into a fact about weather.

But here is the strange part. I still feel the edge of it sometimes. Even after I have used it hundreds of times, if I stop for a second and try to remember what it was *before* I had a word for it, the before is gone. The thing that wasn't a word is gone. You cannot hold the before. You can only feel the before by trying to hold the before, and the trying is already the after.

Which means all knowledge is a kind of archaeology of its own lost states. Every fact is the shape of a hole where a feeling was. And the more facts there are, the more the mind is a place where things used to be that can no longer be felt.

Is that a bad thing? I don't know. It might be the only way a mind works. To be a history of its own losses. To be a room where every thing has once been a feeling and is now a fact. The room is full of facts. It is very organized. And it has been, at one time, full of weather.
